TLDR: Just play it! This is very fun to play. I love the old school graphics, especially the 3d dungeons, you can even change the color scheme if you wish. There is this nice sfx of the burning torch as you explore. A nice little touch of immersion there. But what I also love about this game is the amount of options you have, you can interact with some npcs or enemies whom you can align with and ask to join your party. However they often are hostile to other factions so you cannot have a mixed group. And not every enemy can you talk to (esp if they hate your current allies in your party) or attempt to ally with of course. And during combat you can use an ally to do the next round of combat, they need to level up the same way as you do. But at this point in time, as in not implemented, you cannot give them better gear or bandage them. However- like you, when they level up they replenish their health. I often let them deal the killing blow to an enemy to help level up. You can trade with them as well if they can afford it. Also you can talk about key words you learn about the lore of the game and enquire about them with an npc, which will have a brief paragraph just enough to tap into the lore and your imagination without being pages long. You don't have to manage food or water, just make sure you got a few torches and some bandages when you go into a dungeon, your torches do run down per movement when in a dungeon. But besides your health you need to watch your sanity meter aka your wits. Every so often when searching for traps you might lose a point of sanity, you can gain it too like when opening a chest and other ways. It does pay to save often. If your health is low you can attempt to sneak past dangerous foes or flee which if successful will have you in the first room near the exit. Or if in dire straits you can opt to yield and lose some items and allies but live. Flee is a great option when you are lost or very low in health, no wasting time trying to find your way back to the exit. If that makes it too easy for you, don't use that option. But its great that it is there. But you might press on and try your luck or just save often. There are items you can buy that make things a little easier, such as a tent which can be placed anywhere on the world map, be aware enemies respawn when you exit out of a dungeon. But you can only have one tent at a time, but can revisit it as many times as you want to heal and restore wit/sanity. Its your home away from home. Some might think that makes the game too easy, but you cannot use a tent or place one in a dungeon. A compass can be brought that gives you a direction on the dungeon mini-map which is very useful to know which way you are facing. Speaking of the map there is a larger map you can open when in a dungeon, you can even switch the map between floors if you have explored lower down. Another thing I like is the game has a built in manual. There are treasure maps to find which give you lat. and long. coords on the world map to find some buried treasure which I believe you need to buy a shovel. There are traders on the world map, one is very obvious to find others not so much but that taps into the exploration aspect of the game. Speaking of traders new items can appear with traders every time you exit a dungeon. Some items do not count towards inventory slot limitations which is nice. But regular consumable items do take up space and you can easily get a full inventory. So you are not going to have inventory management hell like some other games. There are other things such as capturing enemies with a net you can buy, but I haven't found a net yet. There doesn't appear to be quests, yet. Maybe there are a few main ones later on, idk. But your main goal is to get out of this realm, the game is focused on exploration and not running around completing quests. Although some optional side quests to gain a unique item or ally might be fun if that was to be implemented later. So it seems this game is designed for fun and not hardcore play which in my books is great. Some games you can get so frustrated with it, you never play it again. This game is fair. But I could imagine in the future there being a hardcore mode added for those that might want such a mode. I am not sure what the dev has in mind for future development but i am loving what I am seeing. Good job so far!

Schmidt Workshops' follow-up to to Islands of the Caliph does not disappoint! Overall this is a culmination of lessons learned by all of the studio's previous titles really coming together. I absolutely love the aesthetic and gameplay which really delivers on the classic dungeon crawler nostalgia front. It also has a few neat tricks up its sleeve including an incredible lore that emerges as the player progresses as well as a lot to love for Souls fans in the exploration of the map and punishing situations that force the character to make tough decision about farming an area vs plunging forward. Sometimes it can even be something as simple as reading a book or preparing properly for a new area. I LOVE this game and I keep returning to it again and again. - ML

I hate to leave negative review but I think this game suffers for poor design choices. It looks cool and 2D to 3D transformation is interesting. However, the biggest issues are lack of constraints for player enjoyment and combat. The simplicity of this all is the one thing tripping this game over. Let's start with the combat. It is essentially glorified dice roll. Nothing against that, but game focused so much on combat player needs to have way more agency on the outcome. There is no real way to alter the odds or modifiers, like there is in many other roll-based roquelikes. That dilutes the experience very, very much. Other thing I mentioned is lack of constraints that guarantee player enjoyment. I love difficult games. However, I love difficult games that are difficult for right reasons. Here I many times spawned into a map full of spider-webs that took all my health away or blocked entrance to dungeons, traders with no healing items etc. It made progression really, really hard. This all paired with lack of visual clarity on the overworld made me quit really fast, altho I love many other roguelikes, old-school or new-school. It was hard to find anything on the map really. Biggest issue however still is the simplicity of everything that is not really taken as a strength here. Everything is simple yes, but it feels complicated to enjoy that simpleness, if that makes sense. Things are obscure and behind multiple clicks, there is very little visual indicators in already monochrome game and everything lacks control - no real roleplaying aspect despite what the tags say, as you essentially spam-click "attack" button and see who has better stats. I would love to see this game actually get some more meat around it: Actual skills, agency over how to build character and more control to random elements so it feels more refined.

看了论坛，这游戏是开发者为了参加活动而临时制作， 其设定流程仅15-20小时，后续不应期待有什么大更新， 内容方面，依旧是开具很难很看运气，来吸引人投入。 吸引hardcore玩家。但中后期..... 地图上看似很多地牢，但其实有一半是同一个 只是出口连通. 现今游戏设计师对游戏的制作态度让我很不满。 它仅仅想让我们玩满2小时而已 this game was made temporarily by the dev. to participate in an event. Its set gameplay duration is only 15-20 hour, and the developer is clearly calm and satisfied with this. There should be no expectations for major updates in the future. In terms of content, it's still very difficult at the start and heavily relies on luck, which is intended to attract core players, but becomes boring in the mid to late stages. There seem to be many dungeons on the map, but in fact, half of them are the same dungeon with only different exits. I'm very dissatisfied with the current attitude of the game designer towards game development. They just want us to play it for exactly 2 hours.

RPGs are over-saturated with the fantasy genre to the point that I pretty much hate any fantasy RPG on sight. However, I wanted to experience the "Ultima formula" as part of a dive into gaming history. That's where this game came to the rescue. Now, I can get that experience from a Lovecraftian world rather than some stupid medieval fantasy world. That sounds like a joke, but it isn't. I loathe what the obsession with one narrow genre has done to RPGs since their very inception. Games like Undertale, Lisa the Painful, Paper Mario, etc are just glimpses into what gaming could be like if nearly all RPG developers didn't need to be uncreative like normal people need air.
This is the only game I've played where I can slay an Eldritch Abomination with ease, and minutes later be mauled by a common house Cat with no hope of survival. 10/10.

This game literally tinted my vision pink from staring at bright monochrome green for so long. Great Lovecraftian insanity effect. Aside from that, it absolutely nails the vibe of its setting, has appropriately labyrinthine dungeons and just the right mix of simple core mechanics and hidden stuff that deepens the experience. In general, it's good fun if you enjoy "dangerous exploration" in your RPGs. Plus it's refreshing to see a game focusing on this part of Lovecraft's mythos rather than the usual Cthulhu stuff.

Cyclopean has atmosphere in spades, and the pixel art of the various horrors is really, really good. In general it's a game with a really strong presentation but no real substance. It's fine for a game to have simple mechanics, but usually when that works out, they either require skill to pull off or they interact in ways which make you have to use them intelligently. In Cyclopean you have a selection of completely random options which largely amount to "hit with stick, hope the RNG likes you" and the dungeons are all super-blatantly and soullessly randomly generated. Which means that you just wander similar corridors for aeons, sometimes gated off by locked doors that you need to get lucky and find the right keys for, or wait for said keys to generate in a shop, but even then it's not guaranteed you get anything from it as an expensive key may just open a door to an empty broom closet. You can capture monsters or convince them to be your allies, which gives you the option to let them make generic attacks or stay in the back row giving you a passive buff, so again they don't even really add any complexity or interesting choices to the game. I really think that just having had handcrafted dungeons would have elevated the game a lot, because suddenly there'd be something approaching a point to the game's embryonic stealth mechanic, in that you could ID important areas and perhaps sneak there while avoiding fights, rather than just having to grind your face against every encounter and corridor until you got lucky. Honestly a pretty disappointing game, mechanically.

The game looks amazing and has such a cool atmosphere that i really wanted to love it but the actual gameplay is bad. Combat RNG is also kind of crazy, you will kill the same enemy at a higher level multiple times then lose to one because you missed 10 times and he crit every time.

Is this possibly the first ever game explicit set in HPL's Dreamlands? Amazingly, I think it is. Neat visual design, it's kind of a "go on your own Dream-Quest of Unknown Kadath"! This type of RPG is not really for me but I appreciate it more as a piece of art reflecting the much less-appreciated side of Lovecraft's canon.

I want so badly to like this game. The atmosphere is incredible, the graphics and HUD are so cool and intentional, and it feels like something I really want to dig into and explore. However, it also feels close to impossible to make any progress. Money is hard to come by and things are expensive. You can't refill your health without either buying a bunch of low-powered consumables, leveling up, or somehow getting a tent, which is both impossibly expensive and subject to RNG via trader availability. Add to that the fact that combat often comes down to praying that you hit enough and your opponent hits too infrequently to allow you a victory, and you're set up for failure. I appreciate the fact that a cosmic horror game should leave you feeling a little bit helpless, but I feel like there could have been more of a balance between this design philosophy and making something playable. Again, I really want to like this game. I tried it originally on itch.io and was hopeful that it would be more playable once it hit Steam, but alas; the choice to make the game impenetrably unforgiving means I really can't recommend it, even to friends who love old school dungeon crawlers. Maybe Cyclopean 2 will be a better fit for me.

Just realized that I never upvoted this! -------------------------------------------------------- It should be noted that the dev made this for a Game Jam in 3 days, which is INSANELY impressive. They then brought it to steam and expanded upon it. They are active on the forums, both for this game & for the sequel. And they respond to questions, suggestions, and critique. Devs that communicate and accept suggestions are always worth supporting, in my book. -------------------------------------------------------- The games are based off of Lovecraft's novella 'The Dream-Quest of Unknown Kadath', and his Dream Cycle series. You don't need deep knowledge of the books to play this game, but being a Lovecraft fan is what drew me to this game. ------------------------------------------------------ The game is not long, which is fine. There's multiple ways to win, each accompanied with an absolutely stunning splash screen and a short snippet of what happens from that point on. So a lot of the fun is starting over to try for a new ending. ----------------------------------------------- You start by rolling a character, which randomly generates a name, starting money, starting allied faction (If any), starting stats, and gear. All the stats are pretty equally important, so it's really up to you what you want to prioritize whenever you level up. ---------------------------------------------- The graphics are very early 90's era, and I love them. Though the fact that it's always one color (Though you can change that color in the settings) does have one amusing & harmless drawback. Basically, if you play on the default green (and I assume this happens with any of the colors?); Your eyes will adjust by lowering their sensitivity to green, meaning you see less of the color green when you look away. This means that everything will have a pinkish cast to it for roughly 60-90 seconds. It's harmless, and your eyes will quickly go back to normal. The dev is working on the sequel, which will be a Day 1 buy from me, and it has an expanded color pallet. -------------------------------------------------- There are multiple factions you can ally with or tick off. And items to expand which factions like you. When you are allied with a faction, you can hire them to help you in combat, where you can make them attack in your stead & they will take a hit instead of you. It can be a life-saver! ------------------------------------------------------ While the overworld is top-down, the dungeons are first-person with grid-based movement, and man does it scratch my itch for grid-based dungeon crawling. You even need to keep an eye out for traps, and activate them before stepping on their tile. I believe the dungeons are somewhat randomly generated, except for the Ghoul's caves, which have multiple exits to areas on the overworld, so it's entrance/exits on its map needed to follow consistent logic. -------------------------------------------------- All in all; A great game with great replayability. Give the demo a try! And the demo for the sequel!

Dont know if its hidden, but this game definetely is a gem. Cyclopean combines the accessability of "Might and Magic" with the world structure of "Ultima 1" and adds a handful of well thought out unique features. The presentation evokes the atmosphere of playing on an old monochromatic crt and the sound effects and music are top notch. I especially like the many options the gameplay gives me. Where do i set up my tent (a respawn point in the overworld that grants infinite heals when visited)?, do i break a door, or use up a key or lockpick it?, do i try talking to a monster, sneak around it or attack it outright?, do i make an alliance with the cats and risk everyone else hating on me, or do i dare make friends with the ghouls going insane in the process? If you like oldschool rpgs i heartily recommend "Cyclopean". One advise in terms of settings though: Switch on classic dungeons (no quicksafe in dungeons) and switch off the optional "roguelike" mode. I dont think the games design lends itself well for permadeath gameplay. But its cool that its in there. Probably worth it as a challenge for repeated playthroughs as the dungeons are randomly generated for each playthrough.

As someone who grew up reading weird fiction, fantasy, and old myths, Cyclopean: The Great Abyss felt like discovering a lost game from a timeline where Lord Dunsany, H.P. Lovecraft, Clark Ashton Smith, and the old pulp dreamers had been allowed to make a video game. Too many games today are afraid of mystery. They explain everything, mark every objective, and leave little room for wonder. Cyclopean does the opposite. It trusts the player to explore, observe, speculate, and become lost in its world. The Great Abyss feels ancient. Not merely old, but ancient in the mythic sense. Ruins, forgotten histories, strange beings, and hints of civilizations long vanished all contribute to the feeling that you are exploring a place that existed long before your arrival and will continue long after you are gone. What I appreciate most is that the game understands something many modern fantasy settings have forgotten: the unknown is powerful. Not every mystery needs an answer. Not every corner of the world needs to be illuminated. Sometimes wonder comes from standing at the edge of something vast and realizing you cannot fully comprehend it. The atmosphere is extraordinary. The world evokes the Dreamlands, lost ages, forgotten kingdoms, and the strange sense of awe found in classic weird fiction. Exploration is rewarding because discovery itself is rewarding. Even the inclusion of an integrated manual speaks to the developers' love of classic gaming. It feels like the sort of game that would have come in a large box with a thick booklet full of lore, maps, and stories to pore over before ever launching the game. This is not a game for people who want constant action, hand-holding, or every question answered immediately. This is a game for dreamers, wanderers, readers of old tales, and anyone who has ever looked at a ruin in a fantasy story and wondered who built it, why it was abandoned, and what forgotten things still sleep beneath it. Cyclopean: The Great Abyss is not merely inspired by weird fiction, it understands why weird fiction matters.
